style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare transliterations in amp with Strong's carried in notes; em-dashes used sparingly; transliterations ASCII-normalized relative to the lexicon's spellings; 'the LORD' for YHWH; deity pronouns capitalized.
chapterNote: The pilgrim's arrival psalm -- David's Song of Ascents for the moment the road ends and the feet stand inside the gates. It begins with the gladness of being invited: I rejoiced when they said to me, let us go to the house of the LORD -- worship as something a man is happy to be summoned to. Then the city itself, seen with a pilgrim's fresh eyes: Jerusalem built compact and joined together, the place all the tribes go up, where the thrones of David's house sit for judgment -- one city holding both the altar and the bench, worship and justice under one wall. The last four verses are the prayer the psalm was written to teach: pray for the peace of Jerusalem -- shalom inside her walls, security in her towers -- prayed for the sake of brothers and companions, and for the sake of the house of the LORD our God. The Hebrew even plays the city's name: Yerushalaim, pray for her shalom. Every believer who has ever loved a congregation knows the whole psalm from the inside.

1.text: A song of ascents, of David. Gladness filled me when they said to me, 'Let us go to the LORD's house.'
1.amp: A Song [shir] of degrees [maaloth -- of ascents] of David. I was glad [samach] when they said [amar] unto me, 'Let us go [yalak] into the house [bayith] of the LORD [YHWH].'
1.notes: samachti -- I rejoiced -- at an invitation to worship: the psalm's whole temperature in its first word. The bet YHWH (H1004) is the destination of the maaloth (H4609), the climbing songs, and the pilgrim's gladness is that others said 'let us go' -- worship as a shared errand, not a solitary duty.

2.text: Our feet are standing inside your gates, O Jerusalem.
2.amp: Our feet [regel] shall stand [amad] within your gates [shaar], O Jerusalem [Yerushalaim].
2.notes: The arrival verse: after the road, the regel amad (H7272, H5975) -- feet planted and standing still inside the shearim (H8179). The participle catches the moment itself: standing, now, here. Every ascent-song aims at this sentence.

3.text: Jerusalem, built as a city knit closely together as one --
3.amp: Jerusalem [Yerushalaim] is builded [banah] as a city [ir] that is compact [chabar -- joined, bound] together [yachad]:
3.notes: The pilgrim looks up at the walls: banah (H1129), built -- chabar yachad (H2266, H3162), joined into one, no gaps. Architecture as theology: the city's tightness pictures the people's unity, and the Psalter's 'together' (yachad) is the same word Psalm 133 will sing.

4.text: where the tribes go up, the tribes of the LORD -- a testimony for Israel -- to give thanks to the name of the LORD.
4.amp: Whither [sham] the tribes [shebet] go up [alah], the tribes of the LORD [Yah], unto the testimony [eduth -- the ordinance, the appointed witness] of Israel [Yisrael], to give thanks [yadah] unto the name [shem] of the LORD [YHWH].
4.notes: The shebatim (H7626), the tribes, alah (H5927) -- going UP, the pilgrim-verb, three times a year as the edut (H5715) of Israel appointed (cf. Deuteronomy 16:16). They are called shibte Yah, the LORD's own tribes: the nation's identity defined by whom it climbs to thank.

5.text: For there the thrones for judgment are set, the thrones of the house of David.
5.amp: For there are set ['do sit', yashab, the KJV margin] thrones [kisse] of judgment [mishpat], the thrones of the house [bayith] of David.
5.notes: The city holds two houses: the LORD's (v. 1) and David's -- altar and bench in one wall. kisot le-mishpat (H3678, H4941), thrones for judgment: worship and justice co-located, as the covenant intended. The Son of David would one day claim both seats at once (cf. Luke 1:32-33).

6.text: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: 'May those who love you prosper in security.
6.amp: Pray [shaal -- ask, inquire] for the peace [shalom] of Jerusalem [Yerushalaim]: they shall prosper [shalah -- be secure, at ease] that love [ahab] you.
6.notes: The psalm's assignment, with wordplay the ear was meant to catch: shaalu shelom Yerushalaim -- ask the shalom (H7965) of the city whose very name ends in shalom. And the promise for the pray-ers: yishlayu (H7951), they shall be secure, ohavayikh -- those who love you. Loving God's city is itself a safe investment.

7.text: May peace be inside your ramparts, and quiet security inside your citadels.'
7.amp: Peace [shalom] be within your walls [chel -- your ramparts], and prosperity [shalvah -- security, ease] within your palaces [armon -- your citadels].
7.notes: The prayer itself, in the pilgrim's own words: shalom in the chel (H2426), the outer rampart, and shalvah (H7962) in the armenot (H759), the citadels within -- peace from the perimeter to the keep. A blessing spoken over the whole cross-section of a city.

8.text: For the sake of my brothers and my companions, I will say now, 'Peace be within you.'
8.amp: For my brethren [ach] and companions' [rea] sakes, I will now say [dabar], 'Peace [shalom] be within you.'
8.notes: The motive is people, not stones: achai ve-reai (H251, H7453), the brothers and friends who live behind the walls. The pilgrim who prays for Jerusalem is praying for faces. The church's version: love the congregation, and you will find yourself praying for its peace unbidden.

9.text: Because of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek out your good.
9.amp: Because of the house [bayith] of the LORD [YHWH] our God [Elohim] I will seek [baqash] your good [tov].
9.notes: The deepest motive last: le-maan bet YHWH Elohenu -- for the sake of the house that makes the city matter. baqash tov (H1245, H2896): not merely wishing well but seeking the city's good as a project. The psalm ends where it began, at the bayith, and hands every pilgrim a lifelong assignment (cf. Jeremiah 29:7; Hebrews 12:22).
